The three-vortex motion is reduced in two stages: first to Jacobi coordinates, then by a Nambu reduction.
The reduced dynamics evolve on a two-dimensional manifold whose topology depends on the sign of parameter κ₂.
For κ₂ > 0, the phase space is a sphere; for κ₂ < 0, it is the upper sheet of a two-sheeted hyperboloid.
Previous reductions by Gröbli and Aref used pairwise distances and had singularities at collinear vortex configurations.
The new reduction removes singularities and provides a standard phase plane for analysis.
The system conserves Hamiltonian energy, linear impulse, and angular impulse.
The paper applies the reduction to three identical vortices and to vortex-dipole scattering.
Invariant manifolds of equilibria in the reduced system correspond to boundaries between direct and exchange scattering.
Changes in the scattering diagram as vortex circulation varies correspond to bifurcations of equilibria.
Jacobi coordinates are canonical transformations that simplify the three-body vortex problem.
Nambu brackets generalize Poisson brackets and allow a Hamiltonian description on reduced manifolds.
The angular impulse Θ acts as a Casimir invariant in the Nambu bracket formulation.
Collinear vortex configurations correspond to singularities in previous coordinate systems but are regular in the new system.
The reduction assumes non-vanishing total circulation and positive circulations for two vortices without loss of generality.
The new coordinates enable clearer geometric and dynamical systems reasoning about vortex motion.
The Hamiltonian in reduced coordinates involves logarithms of distances and quadratic terms weighted by circulations.
The paper translates and builds upon classical results from Gröbli’s 1877 thesis and Aref’s trilinear coordinate approach.
The scattering problem involves a dipole of vortices with circulations (1,1,-1) interacting with a stationary vortex.
The phase space topology influences the nature of vortex interactions and scattering outcomes.
The new reduction may have applications in understanding turbulence and quantum fluids.
